title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
body: Technique for identifying and capturing changes (inserts, updates, deletes) to data in source systems in real-time. Enables efficient data replication without full table scans. Critical for feeding data lakes with fresh transactional data.

title: Debezium
body: Open-source CDC platform that connects to databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB) and streams changes to Kafka or other targets. Provides exactly-once semantics and schema evolution handling.

title: Fivetran
body: Managed cloud data integration platform supporting 400+ pre-built connectors. Simplifies data movement from SaaS apps, databases, and data warehouses to lakes/warehouses. Handles CDC, schema management, and quality validation.

title: Data Integration
body: Process of combining data from multiple heterogeneous sources into a unified view. Includes extraction (from source systems), transformation (cleaning, enriching), and loading (into target systems). Core capability of data pipelines.

metadata.source: Data Warehouse and ETL Best Practices

title: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)
body: Traditional data pipeline pattern: Extract data from sources, Transform (clean, enrich, aggregate) in a staging area, Load into target warehouse. Slower than ELT but ensures data quality before loading.

title: ELT (Extract, Load, Transform)
body: Modern data pipeline pattern: Extract from sources, Load into target (raw zone), Transform using target system's compute. Faster than ETL; leverages cloud warehouse's power. Common in Databricks/Snowflake architectures.

title: Managed Connectors
body: Pre-built, maintainable integrations provided by data platforms (Databricks, Fivetran, Stitch) that handle complex source systems. Eliminate custom code for common sources like Salesforce, ServiceNow, or Stripe.

title: Data Sharing (Delta Sharing)
body: Databricks' protocol for securely sharing live Delta tables across organizations and clouds without copying data. Enables controlled, auditable data access between companies while maintaining single source of truth.

title: Kafka
body: Distributed event streaming platform. Acts as a central hub for real-time data pipelines. Sources publish events (changes) to topics; consumers (data lakes, analytics systems) subscribe and process streams.

title: Event Streaming
body: Continuous flow of events (state changes) from source systems. Used for real-time data pipelines, triggered actions, and audit trails. Kafka is the de facto platform for event streaming.

title: Stream Processing
body: Real-time analysis and transformation of data streams. Frameworks like Spark Structured Streaming, Flink, or Kafka Streams process events as they arrive, enabling real-time analytics and decision-making.

title: Spark Structured Streaming
body: Apache Spark API for stream processing with batch-like programming model. Handles incremental micro-batching of streaming data, enables stateful aggregations and joins with batch data.

title: Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS) / Exactly-Once Processing
body: Guarantee that each message is processed exactly once, not lost and not duplicated. Critical for data integrity in financial systems. Debezium and Kafka provide EOS; Spark defaults to at-least-once.

title: At-Least-Once Semantics
body: Guarantee that each message is processed at least once (may be duplicated). Simpler than exactly-once but requires idempotent processing. Common in cost-sensitive systems.

title: Idempotency / Idempotent Processing
body: Property where processing the same message multiple times produces the same result as processing once. Essential for fault-tolerant systems. Example: INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.

title: Data Freshness
body: How recent/up-to-date data in a system is compared to the source. Real-time streaming achieves high freshness; daily batch updates have lower freshness. Critical for time-sensitive decisions.

title: Latency (in Data Pipelines)
body: Time delay between when data is created in source system and when it's available for analysis. Streaming achieves low latency (seconds); batch has higher latency (hours/days). Trade-off with cost and complexity.

title: Throughput
body: Volume of data processed per unit time (records/sec, MB/sec). Determines pipeline capacity and cost. Batch processing achieves high throughput; real-time streaming prioritizes latency over throughput.

title: Schema Evolution
body: Handling changes to data structure over time (new fields, changed types). CDC systems like Debezium track schema changes; data warehouses (Delta Lake) support schema inference and additive changes.

title: Data Validation / Data Quality
body: Checks ensuring data meets quality standards (completeness, uniqueness, format, range). Integrated into pipelines via frameworks like Great Expectations or dbt tests to catch issues early.

title: Great Expectations
body: Open-source data validation framework for building and testing data pipelines. Defines expectations (assertions) about data, validates batches, and produces data quality reports.

title: Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
body: Separate queue for messages that failed processing. Enables safe handling of bad data without halting pipeline. Operators investigate DLQ messages and fix/re-process them.

title: Replication
body: Copying data from a source system (database, API) to a target system (data lake, warehouse) keeping them synchronized. Can be full (initial copy) or incremental (ongoing changes via CDC).

title: Reverse ETL
body: Moving data from warehouse back to operational systems (CRM, marketing tools). Enables data-driven operations like personalizing offers based on analytics. Growing practice in modern data stacks.

title: Cross-Cloud Consumption
body: Accessing and using data across multiple cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP). Databricks supports Delta Sharing for cross-cloud data access. Enables agility and multi-vendor strategies.

title: API-First Data Integration
body: Designing data integration around APIs (REST, GraphQL) rather than direct database access. Improves security, maintainability, and enables SaaS integrations. Opposite of direct SQL access.
